overview.headline: How a bill moves through committee, voting and presidential review

keyPoints.point: Students learn that Congress is the lawmaking branch of the federal government.
keyPoints.quote: Congress is the lawmaking branch of the federal government.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that a bill is a proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law that can be amended.
keyPoints.quote: A bill is a proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that the president can approve a bill and sign it into law or refuse approval with a veto.
keyPoints.quote: The president can approve the bill and sign it into law.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that only the House can initiate tax and revenue-related legislation while only the Senate handles nominations and treaties.
keyPoints.quote: Only the House can initiate tax and revenue-related legislation

keyTerms.gloss: proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law that members of Congress can introduce
keyTerms.quote: A bill is a proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law.

keyTerms.gloss: group of members assigned to research and discuss a bill and make changes
keyTerms.quote: Once a bill is introduced, it is assigned to a committee whose members will research, discuss, and make changes to the bill.

keyTerms.gloss: presidential refusal called a veto when refusing to approve a bill
veto by default when a bill remains unsigned while Congress is no longer in session and cannot be overridden
keyTerms.quote: This action is called a pocket veto, and it cannot be overridden by Congress.

keyTerms.gloss: house of Congress that votes on a bill before it moves to the other body
keyTerms.quote: The bill is then put before that chamber to be voted on.
